items.prompt: What does DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) actually require?
choices: Every piece of knowledge or logic should have a single, unambiguous place it lives
No two files may contain any similar-looking code
Every function must be reused in at least two places
Code must be written as compactly as possible
items.explanation: DRY is about knowledge having one home, not about text looking different — a change to that knowledge should only ever need to happen in one place.
items.reference:
DRY
one piece of knowledge
= one place it lives

Why: DRY is about avoiding the same rule living in two places, not about banning similar-looking text.

items.prompt: Why is DRY described as being about 'knowledge,' not just 'text'?
choices: Because two pieces of code can look completely different and still violate DRY, if they encode the same rule in two places
Because DRY only applies to comments, not actual code
Because 'knowledge' just means variable names must match exactly
Because DRY has nothing to do with how code looks
items.explanation: A discount cap written as `100` in one file and `1.0` as a fraction in another can both represent the same rule despite looking nothing alike — DRY cares about that shared rule, not the surface text.
items.reference:
DRY
one piece of knowledge
= one place it lives

Why: DRY is about avoiding the same rule living in two places, not about banning similar-looking text.

items.prompt: A discount cap is written as `100` in one file and as the fraction `1.0` in another, both meant to represent 'never discount more than the full price.' Does DRY consider this a violation?
choices: Yes — it's the same piece of knowledge represented in two places, even though the two representations look different
No, since the two values look nothing alike
No, because DRY only applies to functions, never to constants
Yes, but only if both files are in the same folder
items.explanation: DRY cares about the underlying knowledge, not the surface representation — two different-looking values that must always change together in sync are still the same piece of knowledge duplicated.
items.reference:
DRY
one piece of knowledge
= one place it lives

Why: DRY is about avoiding the same rule living in two places, not about banning similar-looking text.

items.prompt: What makes two pieces of code 'true duplication,' as this unit defines it?
choices: They express the same underlying rule, which should always change together
They happen to be the exact same number of lines
They were written by the same engineer
They both appear in files with similar names
items.explanation: True duplication is about the underlying rule, not surface appearance — two copies of the same rule should always change together when that rule changes.
items.reference:
True duplication
same underlying rule
should always change together

Why: This is exactly what DRY exists to avoid — a rule change that has to be made correctly in multiple places.

items.prompt: Checkout, cart preview, and the admin refund tool all pasted the exact same 'quantity >= 5 gets 10% off' rule. Why is this true duplication?
choices: Because a change to that discount rule should apply to all three places at once, every time
Because all three files have similar filenames
Because the functions were copy-pasted, regardless of what they express
Because it happens to be exactly three occurrences
items.explanation: All three copies encode the identical business rule — the discount policy, not the number of copies or the filenames, is what makes this true duplication.
items.reference:
True duplication
same underlying rule
should always change together

Why: This is exactly what DRY exists to avoid — a rule change that has to be made correctly in multiple places.

items.prompt: What is 'coincidental duplication'?
choices: Two pieces of code that happen to look similar now, but exist for different reasons and will likely change independently
Duplication that occurs completely at random with no cause
Code that's duplicated across exactly two files
Duplication that was introduced by an automated tool
items.explanation: Coincidental duplication looks the same on the surface today, but the two pieces of code represent unrelated rules that just happen to coincide right now.
items.reference:
Coincidental duplication
looks similar now
different reasons, will diverge later

Why: Merging these into one function forces the shared function to grow branches when the two rules inevitably diverge.

items.prompt: A tax calculation and a discount calculation both happen to multiply by a percentage and round to two decimals. Are they automatically true duplication?
choices: No — they may be coincidental duplication if they represent different rules that just happen to look alike
Yes, since the code is structurally identical
Yes, because both involve percentages
No, because tax and discounts always use different data types
items.explanation: Looking alike isn't the test — tax and discounts are governed by different rules that will likely change independently, which is exactly what coincidental duplication looks like.
items.reference:
Coincidental duplication
looks similar now
different reasons, will diverge later

Why: Merging these into one function forces the shared function to grow branches when the two rules inevitably diverge.

items.prompt: What is 'premature abstraction'?
choices: Extracting a shared function or class before there's real evidence the duplication is the true kind
Writing an abstraction that's too short
Using a design pattern from a textbook
Refactoring code that has no tests
items.explanation: Premature abstraction jumps to extraction before enough real evidence exists to tell true duplication from coincidental duplication, often producing something more tangled than what it replaced.
items.reference:
Premature abstraction
extracted before real evidence exists
often more tangled than the duplication it replaced

Why: Without enough real instances, it's a guess about what's constant and what varies, not a verified pattern.

items.prompt: Why can a premature abstraction end up more tangled than the duplication it replaced?
choices: Because it's built on a guess about what's shared, before real instances reveal what actually varies
Because abstractions are always slower to run than duplicated code
Because premature abstractions always contain more lines of code
Because it removes the need for any documentation
items.explanation: Extracting too early means guessing at the shape of the shared rule — when reality turns out different, the abstraction has to bend to accommodate it, often via flags or branches.
items.reference:
Premature abstraction
extracted before real evidence exists
often more tangled than the duplication it replaced

Why: Without enough real instances, it's a guess about what's constant and what varies, not a verified pattern.

A function that's longer than 20 lines
A function with more than one return statement
A function name that contains a verb
items.explanation: A flag like `isBulk` or `isLoyalty` used to branch inside a shared function is the concrete sign that two unrelated rules got stitched together behind one signature.
items.reference:
The flag warning sign

Why: Every future caller now has to understand both branches to safely use either one.

Because functions should never take more than two parameters
Because boolean parameters are always a performance problem
Because `isBulk` is a poorly chosen variable name

items.reference:

items.prompt: According to the rule of three, what should happen the first two times a piece of logic appears to be duplicated?
choices: Usually leave it separate, but take note — there isn't enough evidence yet to know if it's true or coincidental duplication
Extract a shared function immediately on the second occurrence
Delete one of the two copies immediately
Rewrite both copies to use a design pattern
items.explanation: Two occurrences alone don't provide enough evidence to distinguish true duplication from coincidental duplication — extracting too early is a guess, not a verified pattern.
items.reference:
Rule of three
1: nothing to compare
2: not enough evidence, usually wait
3+: extract, shape is now clear

Why: A third real occurrence reveals what's actually constant vs. what varies, which two alone can't show.

items.prompt: Why does the third occurrence of a duplicated pattern provide meaningfully more evidence than the second?
choices: It reveals what actually varies between the instances, making the shape of the real abstraction visible
Three is a mathematically special number for abstraction
It doesn't provide more evidence — two and three are equally sufficient
It means the code has been reviewed by three different engineers
items.explanation: With only two instances, it's hard to tell what's coincidentally the same versus what's actually the fixed shape of the rule — a third instance clarifies which parts are constant.
items.reference:
Rule of three
1: nothing to compare
2: not enough evidence, usually wait
3+: extract, shape is now clear

Why: A third real occurrence reveals what's actually constant vs. what varies, which two alone can't show.

items.prompt: What is the actual test this unit gives for whether two pieces of similar-looking code should be merged?

Are the two pieces of code exactly the same number of lines?
Were the two pieces of code written on the same day?
Do the two pieces of code use the same variable names?
items.explanation: The test is about whether a rule change must always apply to both places — not about surface-level similarity like line count or naming.

The real test

no/unsure → coincidental, leave separate

Why: Surface similarity is not the same question as "do these represent the same rule."

Because merging always slows down the program
Because identical code can never actually be merged successfully
Because coincidental duplication is illegal under most style guides
items.explanation: The moment the two rules diverge, the merged function has to serve both anyway — usually by growing a parameter or branch just to keep working for both original callers.
items.reference:
The real test

items.prompt: When coincidental duplication gets merged and the two rules later diverge, what actually happens to the 'second change' that would otherwise have been a second, separate edit?
choices: It moves inside the shared function as a new branch or flag, instead of being a second independent function
It disappears entirely — the change is no longer needed
It automatically gets applied to both original call sites without any new code
It becomes impossible to make at all
items.explanation: The abstraction doesn't prevent the second change from happening — it relocates that change inside the shared function, where it now has to coexist with, and not break, the first caller's behavior too.
items.reference:
Where the change goes

it moves inside the shared function instead

Why: A change relocated inside a shared function often becomes harder, since it now has to avoid breaking the other caller too.

items.prompt: Why can a change relocated inside a shared function be harder than the same change made to a separate, unshared function?

Because shared functions always run slower
Because separate functions can never be tested
Because shared functions cannot be edited by more than one engineer
items.explanation: A change made inside a function used by multiple callers has to be made carefully enough not to alter behavior for callers who didn't ask for that change.
items.reference:
